passage:
Monday, in the hostel canteen, Rafiq showed Vikas an article that criticised the star Vikas adored. “Fake,” Vikas said before he reached the second paragraph. Neha and Sam, at the same table, kept eating and said nothing.
Wednesday, late at night. Vikas replayed the star’s interview clips and felt as if the star were speaking straight to him. He typed a long reply to a stranger who had criticised the star.
Saturday. Rafiq asked lightly, “Would he even know your name?” Vikas snapped, “That’s not the point,” and walked out. In the corridor his chest felt tight, as if Rafiq had said something about him.

qa.q: What did Vikas say about the article on Monday?
qa.a: Vikas said, “Fake,” before reaching the second paragraph.

qa.q: Why did Vikas's chest feel tight after Rafiq's question?
qa.a: Criticising the star felt like criticising Vikas, and the question about being known touched something painful. His snapping reply and tight chest suggest hurt more than anger.

qa.q: What small step could help Vikas after that Saturday?
qa.a: Vikas could read the article slowly and separate what it says about the star's actions from how he feels about himself. He could then decide what he still admires.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt after Vikas walked out?
qa.a: Rafiq may have felt surprised and a bit guilty, since the question was asked lightly and a strong reaction was not expected. The passage does not say for sure.

grounding: Shows a young adult defending an admired star automatically because criticism feels personal, with a one-sided closeness.

passage:
Yash, come and sit. When I was twenty, I loved a film hero more than my own opinion. I’m Preeti, and I can say that now, but then I couldn’t. My college friend Anita once said his latest film was dull, and I didn’t speak to her for a week.
I wrote him a letter and never got a reply. I read every magazine and felt he knew me. Anita just waited. After a week she came with two tickets for his next film and said, “Let’s watch, then argue.”
In the dark I saw the same dull scene she meant. I said nothing, but my face was hot.

qa.q: How long did Preeti stay silent with Anita?
qa.a: Preeti did not speak to Anita for a week.

qa.q: Why did Preeti's face feel hot in the dark theatre?
qa.a: Preeti saw the same dull scene Anita had meant and felt uncomfortable because Anita had been right. Admitting it would mean the hero was not perfect.

qa.q: Which choice of Anita's helped Preeti most?
qa.a: Anita waited a week and then brought two tickets and proposed watching first and arguing later. She kept the friendship without forcing Preeti to admit anything.

qa.q: How might Anita have felt during that week of silence?
qa.a: Anita may have felt hurt and puzzled that a small opinion cost the friendship. Waiting and then bringing tickets suggests she still valued Preeti.

grounding: An elder recalls idealising a film hero so strongly that criticism felt personal, until a friend's patience opened a gap.

passage: In the small town of Kalimpong, Indu watched every video by the speaker Sameer Batra, three times a day. She wrote his lines on her wall: 'Winners never rest.' She felt he was speaking straight to her, as if he knew about her failed exam and her mother's tea stall. When Pema said one of his videos made fun of poor people, Indu snapped, 'You don't know him!' Pema said quietly, 'Neither do you.' Indu stormed home. That night she typed a long comment under his latest video, pouring out her heart. It got three likes and no reply. Indu stared at it for a long time, feeling foolish and still, somehow, loyal.

qa.q: What line did Indu write on her wall?
qa.a: 'Winners never rest.'

qa.q: Why did Indu snap at Pema?
qa.a: She felt defensive and hurt, as if criticism of Sameer Batra were criticism of herself.

qa.q: What might help Indu keep what's useful without losing judgement?
qa.a: Take the ideas that help her, notice when a video mocks people, and lean on real friends like Pema who actually know her.

qa.q: What was Pema trying to tell Indu with 'Neither do you'?
qa.a: That the closeness is one-sided; Pema cares and wanted Indu to see the speaker doesn't know her.

grounding: A young woman defends a public speaker as if criticism were personal, though he does not know she exists.

passage: In their shared flat in São Paulo, Priscila had a poster of the city councillor Lucas Prado above her desk. She had volunteered for his campaign, and after he once shook her hand at a rally, she felt they had a real connection. When news came out that his office had quietly cancelled funding for a children's library, her roommate Jamal read it aloud. 'That's not him,' Priscila said instantly. 'It's his staff.' 'He signed it,' Jamal said, showing her the document. Priscila's cheeks burned; it felt like Jamal was attacking her. She went to her room and wrote Prado a long message. An automatic reply thanked her for her support. She read it twice. For the first time, she noticed he didn't even know her name.

qa.q: What did Prado's office cancel funding for?
qa.a: A children's library.

qa.q: Why did Priscila's cheeks burn when Jamal showed the document?
qa.a: She felt attacked and defensive, as if criticism of Prado were criticism of her.

qa.q: What could Priscila do to keep her values and her judgement?
qa.a: Keep supporting ideas she believes in while looking at facts like the signed document, instead of defending Prado automatically.

qa.q: How might Jamal feel after Priscila leaves the room?
qa.a: Probably uncomfortable and worried, since Jamal only showed a document and she took it personally.

grounding: A young adult defends a public figure whatever he does, feeling a closeness that is entirely one-sided.

passage: In the college hostel common room, the TV showed the cricket captain Nikhil Rana refusing to shake an umpire's hand after a bad decision. Half the room booed. Aparna jumped up. 'He was right! That umpire's been against him all series!' Vishal, from the next room, said, 'Still, not shaking hands is poor sport.' Aparna turned on him. 'You've never supported him properly. You wouldn't understand.' She had Rana's jersey, his autobiography with the printed signature inside, and a short recorded message from a fan event that she played before exams. That night she wrote three long posts defending him. Only later, lying in bed, did it strike her: she'd never met him, and she'd just shouted at a friend for him.

qa.q: What did Nikhil Rana refuse to do?
qa.a: Shake an umpire's hand after a bad decision.

qa.q: What did Aparna feel lying in bed?
qa.a: Uneasy and a bit foolish, noticing she had shouted at a real friend to defend someone she'd never met.

qa.q: What could Aparna do the next morning?
qa.a: Apologise to Vishal and allow that she can love Rana's cricket while admitting poor sportsmanship.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt being told 'You wouldn't understand'?
qa.a: Probably stung and dismissed, since Vishal had only made a fair point about sportsmanship.

grounding: A young woman defends a sports star whatever he does, as if criticism of him were criticism of herself.

passage:
Jahnavi,
I'm writing because you walked out of the room last night and I couldn't say it properly.
You called Rehan Sethi arrogant because he walked out of that interview. You don't know him the way I do. I've watched every live, every backstage clip. When he says "my people", I feel he means me. I've defended him in a hundred comment threads. When people criticise him, it feels like they're criticising me, my taste, the four years I've spent loving his music.
I know he doesn't know I exist. I do know that. But last winter, alone in the PG, his voice notes to fans were the only warm thing in my day.
So maybe the interview wasn't great. I still think you were unfair. Can we get chai on Saturday and not talk about him?
Gurleen

qa.q: What did Rehan Sethi do that Jahnavi criticised?
qa.a: He walked out of that interview.

qa.q: Why does criticism of Rehan Sethi feel personal to Gurleen?
qa.a: Gurleen feels so close to him after years of his music that criticism feels like an attack on Gurleen's own taste and self, which stirs hurt and defensiveness.

qa.q: What would you advise Gurleen about the argument with Jahnavi?
qa.a: Admit plainly that the interview wasn't great, as the letter nearly does, and keep the friendship separate from the singer; the chai plan is a good start.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Gurleen's defence of the singer?
qa.a: Jahnavi may feel frustrated that any criticism is taken personally, and worried about how much the singer fills Gurleen's life.

grounding: Gurleen's letter shows a young adult defending a star whatever he does, feeling close to someone who does not know they exist.
